title: The Ear
subtitle: It turns vibrations in the air into the sounds you hear
intro: Point at any part of the ear to see what it does. Press Magnify to lift the tiny bones into view, or start the tour to follow a sound in. Motion is slowed and exaggerated.

structures.name: Pinna
structures.summary: The visible part of the ear. Its folds and ridges collect sound and funnel it into the ear canal.
structures.fact: Its folds bounce sound differently depending on its direction, which helps your brain tell where a sound came from.

structures.name: Ear canal
structures.summary: A tube about 2.5 cm long that carries sound from the pinna to the eardrum. Glands in its skin make earwax, which traps dust and keeps the canal clean.
structures.fact: Its length makes it resonate, boosting sounds in the range where speech is clearest.

structures.name: Eardrum
structures.summary: A thin, cone-shaped sheet of tissue, about as thin as paper, that closes the end of the ear canal. Sound waves make it vibrate.
structures.fact: For the quietest sounds you can hear, it moves by less than the width of an atom.

structures.name: Middle ear
structures.summary: A tiny air-filled chamber behind the eardrum. It holds the three smallest bones in the body.
structures.fact: The bones can only vibrate freely while the chamber is full of air. In glue ear it fills with fluid, and hearing dulls.

structures.name: Malleus
structures.summary: The hammer, the first of the three tiny bones. Its long handle is fixed to the eardrum, so it moves every time the drum does.
structures.fact: Malleus is Latin for hammer. The bone is only about 8 mm long.

structures.name: Incus
structures.summary: The anvil, the middle bone. It passes the vibration from the hammer on to the stirrup, like a tiny lever.
structures.fact: The three bones are named after the tools they resemble: hammer, anvil and stirrup.

structures.name: Stapes
structures.summary: The stirrup, the last of the three bones and the smallest in the body, about 3 mm long. Its flat base presses on the cochlea like a piston.
structures.fact: The eardrum is much larger than the base of the stirrup, so the three bones together boost the pressure roughly twenty times.

structures.name: Cochlea
structures.summary: A fluid-filled tube coiled like a snail shell. Waves in its fluid bend thousands of tiny hair cells, which turn movement into nerve signals.
structures.fact: The three loops above it are the semicircular canals, which sense head movement for balance.

structures.name: Vestibulocochlear nerve
structures.summary: Carries signals from the cochlea, for hearing, and from the balance organs to the brain.
structures.fact: The hearing part alone has about 30,000 nerve fibres.

structures.name: Eustachian tube
structures.summary: A narrow channel from the middle ear to the back of the throat. It opens when you swallow or yawn, keeping the air pressure either side of the eardrum equal.
structures.fact: The pop you feel in your ears in a plane or a lift is this tube opening.

tour.caption: Sound is a vibration in the air. The pinna catches it and funnels it into the ear.
The ear canal guides the sound inwards, and boosts the pitches we use in speech.
At the end of the canal, the sound waves hit the eardrum and make it vibrate. Here it is shown much larger than life.
Behind the drum, the vibration passes to the first of three tiny bones, the hammer.
The hammer hands it to the anvil.
The anvil hands it to the stirrup, the smallest bone in the body. Together the bones make the vibration about twenty times stronger.
The stirrup pushes on the fluid in the cochlea. Waves in the fluid bend tiny hair cells, which turn the movement into electrical signals.
The nerve carries the signals to the brain, which turns them into what you hear.
